product.title: Indonesian 101 - B1
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from A2 to a solid B1 in Bahasa Indonesia, the direct continuation of the A2 module. Every unit has two dialogues, one in the register of the meeting room and one in the register of the kitchen or the group chat, each with a word-for-word translation, grammar notes, vocabulary with pronunciation, four keyed exercises and a wave review of earlier units. At this level Indonesian is for taking part: formal introductions and meeting language, memper- verbs, the full passive system (di-, the pronoun passive, ter-), abstract nouns with ke-an, pe-an and per-an, time nuance with telah, sempat and pernah, relative clauses without the di mana calque, giving opinions, refusing politely, contrast, cause and purpose, news language, respect with beliau and berkenan, particles, idioms and proverbs, loanwords, and focus with -lah, -kah and pun. The story follows Sarah as she coordinates a village tourism project in Sumberwangi near Borobudur: a village meeting on entrance fees, a flood and a fundraising pitch, a radio interview, a visit to the Bupati, a stolen wallet, Rina's Javanese wedding in Jakarta, and the closing festival speech. Includes an A2 review, a B1 grammar summary and word-building tables.

blocks.text: At A1 Indonesian got you through the day. At A2 it let you run a life: a rented house, a landlady, a motorbike, a bank account and a Lebaran spent with someone else's family. **B1 is the level at which you stop surviving in Indonesian and start taking part in it.** You sit in the meeting instead of waiting outside it. You say what you think, and you say it at the right strength. You read the local news about the place you live in, you answer a journalist's questions, you apologise to an elder properly, and you say no to a kind invitation without anybody losing face.

Here is the honest part. The grammar you still need is not large, but it is subtle. Unit 2 brings in **memper-**, the prefix that turns *baik* into *memperbaiki* and *hati* into *memperhatikan*. Unit 3 finishes the **passive system**: *di-* with its endings, the pronoun passive (*Sudah saya baca*) and the three jobs of *ter-*. Unit 4 builds the **abstract nouns** that serious conversation runs on (*keindahan, pembangunan, perbaikan*), and Units 9–10 give you the connectors that hold an argument together. None of it is hard to understand. All of it takes time to reach for without thinking.

The other half of B1 is not grammar at all, and it is where most foreigners stay stuck for years. It is **register and respect**: *beliau* instead of *dia*, *Bapak* and *Ibu* instead of "you", *berkenan* and *mohon izin* (Unit 13). It is **the soft no** (Unit 8), where *kurang bisa* means "no" and *Nanti saya kabari* often means "no" too. It is the **particles** (Unit 14), the *kok, sih, dong* and *deh* that carry the speaker's mood and never appear in a dictionary sentence. And it is **idiom** (Unit 15): the moment someone calls a colleague *kambing hitam* or brings you *buah tangan*, you either follow or you don't.

The story continues from A2. It is 2028, and Sarah now coordinates a community-tourism project, a *desa wisata*, in Sumberwangi, a village in the rice fields a few kilometres from Borobudur, in partnership with Universitas Gadjah Mada. **Pak Harun**, the village head, speaks like a decree at meetings and like a Javanese uncle at home. **Bu Ratna** runs the homestay women's group and misses nothing. **Dr. Lestari Wibowo** of UGM speaks in careful academic Indonesian and expects the reports on time. **Yoga**, the 22-year-old intern, writes brochures full of English and messages full of particles. Mas Bayu, Bu Endang and Dimas are still there in Yogya, and Rina is planning her wedding with Andi.

Over twenty units the village argues about entrance fees (Unit 7), survives a flood (Unit 10), gets into the news (Unit 11), meets the Bupati (Unit 13), loses a room key (Unit 17) and a wallet (Unit 18), and ends with a festival where Sarah presents the results on stage in front of everyone (Unit 20). In between, in Unit 19, she flies to Jakarta for Rina's wedding and stands in the queue at the *pelaminan* with everyone else.

The method has not changed: dialogues first, the word-for-word line under every sentence, short explanations and a lot of practice. What has changed is the length. There are now **two dialogues in every unit**, one in the register of the office or the meeting and one in the register of the kitchen, the phone call or the group chat, because a B1 speaker has to move between the two in the same afternoon.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Give each unit two sittings of about 45 minutes rather than one long evening. At B1 the new material is less about rules and more about feel, and feel comes from coming back.
Read both dialogues **out loud**, twice. The formal one will feel stiff at first: that is the point. Indonesians switch into it the moment they stand up to speak.
Make sure the A2 review at the end of this front matter holds no surprises. If three or more rows in its tables look unfamiliar, go back to A2 first.
Keep the answer key covered until you have finished a whole exercise. Being wrong and finding out why is still the fastest way to learn.

blocks.text: *Selamat belajar*, and welcome to Sumberwangi.
The shape is the same as in A2. Each unit is built to be finished in two sittings of about 45 minutes, and every part has a job.

items: **Two dialogues.** The first runs to 13–15 lines and is usually the public scene: a meeting, an office, an interview. The second, 9–11 lines, moves to a different place and usually a looser register: a phone call, a chat, a neighbour at the gate. Under every line: the natural English, then the word-for-word English.
**Notes.** Six after each dialogue: the things in those lines that would have quietly confused you.
**Grammar boxes.** Three per unit, two after the first dialogue and one after the second, each with a table you can keep.
**Two extra sections.** Word fields, formulas and culture that the dialogues only touch on.
**Wave review.** Five lines from two units back, to rebuild from memory.
**Vocabulary.** Every new word, in the order it appears, with the Say it column and the English.

**Exercises and answer key.** Four sets of six items: a translation, a gap fill, a transformation (make it passive, make it formal, say it the Jakarta way) and a word-order puzzle. That is 480 items across the book.

blocks.title: The word-for-word line
items: Hyphens join what is **one word** in Indonesian but several in English: *kemahalan* → "too-expensive", *dibangun* → "is-built", *uangnya* → "money-the", *menurut* → "according-to".

Particles with no English equivalent stay in square brackets: *[kan] [kok] [sih] [dong] [deh] [lho] [ya] [nih] [tuh] [-lah] [-kah] [pun]*. Unit 14 explains them all; until then, notice where they sit.
The line is deliberately ungrammatical English. It shows you the order Indonesian thinks in, and it is the reason the formal sentences stop looking like puzzles.

blocks.title: The Say it column
items: Syllables are separated by hyphens and the **stressed syllable is in CAPITALS**: *pendapat* puhn-DA-pat, *musyawarah* mu-sya-WA-rah.
**uh** is the schwa, the vowel of "about": *membahas* muhm-BA-has. When the second-last syllable has a schwa, the stress slides to the last one: *empat* uhm-PAT.
**É** is the *e* of "bed" in a stressed syllable, **é** in an unstressed one: *enak* É-nak, *tiket* TI-két.
Everything else is spelled as written: *c* is always "ch", *ng* as in "singer", *ny* as in "canyon".

blocks.text: **The wave.** The third section of every unit is a table of five lines from the unit two before it, English on the left, Indonesian on the right. Cover the right-hand column and rebuild each sentence aloud. Units 1 and 2 reach back to the last two units of A2. Five minutes, every unit, and nothing you learned in March is gone by November.

blocks.title: Two symbols used throughout
items: ⚠️ — a mistake nearly every foreign learner makes here, or a trap that looks like English. Read these twice.
💬 — the everyday spoken form, next to the written one it replaces. At B1 you need both: the first to be understood, the second to understand.

blocks.text: **A realistic pace:** two units a week, one wave review each time and one older unit re-read aloud on the weekend. That is ten weeks to the end of the book. Faster is possible; slower and steadier usually works better.

⚠️ Loanwords take Indonesian affixes like any other root: *mempromosikan, dikoordinasikan, keaktifan*. And watch the false friends: *aktual* is "current", *kantor* is an office.

If you have really worked through these twenty units, not just read them, you are at a **solid B1**. You can follow and take part in a meeting, give an opinion at the strength you mean, turn down a request without offending anyone, read a local news story and answer a journalist, speak to an official with the right respect, cope with the police or a hospital, and stand up and present your work to a room. That is the Indonesian of someone who lives and works in the country, not someone passing through.

What you do not have yet, and what B1 was never meant to give you, is Indonesian for **leading and persuading**: writing that a ministry official will not send back, negotiating a budget across a table, reading literature and legal text, and hearing the difference between Betawi, Javanese, Batak and eastern Indonesian speech.

items: **Indonesian 101 · B2** continues directly from this book. In 2029 Sarah moves back to Jakarta to direct **Program Jembatan**, an Australia–Indonesia education and exchange programme. On the way: *baku* Indonesian and EYD spelling, effective sentences and the formal letter, negotiation and hedging, the media and opinion writing, regional speech and online slang, Chairil Anwar, Pramoedya and the *pantun*, legal and bureaucratic language, speeches and *sambutan*, and the **UKBI**, the official Indonesian proficiency test, which Sarah sits near the end of the book.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, four habits that raise your level fastest from here:

items: **Read one local news story a day.** Regional sites are short and concrete; after a month the headlines of Unit 11 will read themselves.
**Listen to people talking to each other**, not to a camera: podcasts, talk radio, long interviews. That is where the particles of Unit 14 live.
**Write one short paragraph a day in formal Indonesian**, even if nobody reads it: a mini-report, a complaint, a meeting summary. Then say the same thing out loud the way you would to a friend.
**Re-read one unit a week, out loud, in random order.** Twenty weeks later, start again. It costs ten minutes and it keeps everything in this book alive.

blocks.text: And the next time someone in a village hall hands you the microphone and says *Waktu dan tempat kami persilakan*, take it. You know what to say now.
*Sampai jumpa di tingkat B2!*
